newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Cattle Inventory shows tight feeder supplies.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Cattle Inventory shows tight feeder supplies.

text.p: Feeder cattle supplies will tighten and prices should rise in 1997 based on Friday's U.S. Cattle Inventory report, which pointed to the smallest calf crop to be born in the past six years, analysts said.

"What the report assured us, by the size of the starting cow herd, 43.6 million head, was that we will undoubtedly have the smallest calf crop born in 1997 since 1991," said Chuck Levitt, senior livestock analyst for Alaron Trading Corp.
The U.S. Agriculture Department put total cattle in the U.S. as of January 1 at 101.2 million head, down two percent from a year ago.

Total cattle supplies were as expected, but analysts viewed reduced percentages for feeder cattle to be bullish for feeder cattle. USDA reported feeders, heifers, steers and bulls under 500 lbs at 96 percent of last year, well under expectations.

Continuing herd liquidation will weigh on nearby live cattle futures, but the low numbers of feeders and calves in the report will support the deferred live cattle futures, and feeder cattle futures are seen trading another 0.025 to 1.000 cent per lb higher Monday, analysts said.
"The report translates into a starting feeder cattle supply, (feeders) that are not already on feed as of January 1, at 1.2 million head or 3.5 percent smaller than one year earlier," Levitt said.

"Record high corn prices and the impact it had on feeder cattle prices and rancher returns resulted in the largest losses by cow/calf operations since the losses reported in the early '80s" and cut calf production, said Jim Robb from the Livestock Marketing Information Center.

Levitt said the outlook for continued light feeder cattle exports from Mexico will also keep feeder supplies tight and will in turn cut the number of available cattle that can be put onto feedlots. "It is going to be more and more difficult for us to match last year's placement levels on feed because of this smaller feeder cattle supply base," he said.
With placements of cattle onto feedlots seen easing during the year, and already lighter weight cattle on feed, beef production will also ease going into late 1997 and early 1998, Robb said.

"Beef cattle supplies over the next couple of years will continue to tighten. The peak (beef) tonnage was in 1996 and our forecast for 1997 now suggests that beef tonnage will be flat to down slightly," he said.
However, Robb was somewhat pessimistic about expected gains in feeder cattle futures on Monday, based on trading in feeders in response to earlier projections on the report.
"There could be some futures market action, but given the recent strong runup in feeder cattle futures, we're not sure it (report) isn't already built into that market," he said.
